sets.title: Lectures 17 and 18 · 6 of his questions
sets.about: His Lab 9 questions and the heads question he said is on the exam. On November 10 he said the LLM part is kept for the final.

items.question: What is the difference between the input and output of the vowel network and those of an LLM?
items.answer:
The difference is that the vowel network takes in one vector and decides among five categories, while an LLM takes in many vectors and decides among a whole vocabulary.

The vowel network's input is one vector, F1 and F2. Its output decides among five categories.

An LLM's input is many vectors in sequence, such as the words so far. Its output decides among a whole vocabulary for the next item.

items.question: What are heads, and how do they relate to layers?
items.answer: A head is one expert, which is a set of weights that gives its own opinion on how to improve the vectors. Heads sit side by side inside each layer. The layer combines all of its heads' opinions into improved vectors. The layers come one after another from the input to the output. So each layer uses its heads to improve the vectors again.

items.question: Which could be English words: blick, bnick, sblat, splat, dlag, lisk, lisb, lapm, lamp? For each one that could not, name the problem.
items.answer:
Blick, splat, lisk and lamp could be English words.

Bnick, sblat and dlag could not be English words. This is because bn, sb and dl cannot start a syllable in English.

Lisb and lapm could not be English words. This is because sb and pm cannot end a syllable in English.

items.question: Each of these starts an English word: pl_, st_ and th_. What could come next, and what could not?
items.answer:
After pl, only a vowel can come next, as in play. So a consonant such as n cannot come next.

After st, a vowel or r can come next, as in star and street. But l and k cannot come next.

After th, r, w or a vowel can come next, as in three, thwart and thin. But l and n cannot come next.

items.question: What is an agentic system, in terms of LLMs? Describe the example system.
items.answer:
An agentic system is a graph (a set of connected parts) of LLMs (large language models), each with its own job. The LLMs are connected so that one LLM's output becomes the next LLM's input.

In the example system, one LLM outlines, one writes, one critiques, one revises and one produces the final version. The critic and the reviser form a loop. So the draft keeps going back until the critic is satisfied or the limit is reached.

items.question: What does the critic loop do, and what does it prevent that was common in earlier LLMs?
items.answer:
The critic loop sends the draft back and forth between the critic and the reviser until the critic is satisfied. The critic checks each draft, and the reviser fixes the errors the critic finds. So errors are caught and fixed before the answer is shown to the user.

The critic loop prevents hallucination (when an LLM makes up false statements), which was a common problem in earlier LLMs.

sets.title: Lectures 17 and 18 · 34 predicted questions
sets.about: Predicted questions from the Module II study page for Lectures 17 and 18.

items.question: How does the all-or-none behavior of neurons connect to the sigmoid?
items.answer: The all-or-none behavior of neurons is the same idea as the sigmoid. This is because a real neuron is either firing or not firing. The sigmoid turns an inner product into a number near 0 (off) or near 1 (on), with a steep change in between. So an artificial neuron that uses the sigmoid behaves the same way as a real neuron.

items.question: What do parallel and distributed mean in Parallel Distributed Processing?
items.answer:
Parallel means that many neurons calculate their activations at the same time.

Distributed means that the information from the inputs is spread across all the neurons. So the information is not stored in one place.

items.question: What does a single neuron take in and give back? What about a neural network?
items.answer:
A single neuron takes in a vector and gives back one number. That number is the inner product, which is each input multiplied by its weight, with the results added together.

A neural network takes in one vector and gives back a vector of decisions. This is because a neural network repeats the inner product layer after layer. So the network ends with several outputs instead of just one number.

items.question: Why can't the vowel network model a sentence or speech over time?
items.answer: The vowel network cannot model a sentence or speech over time because it takes one static vector and makes one decision. That vector is F1 and F2 (the first two formants) from one moment. But speech changes all the time, and a sentence is many words, one after another. So modeling speech needs a network that works through a sequence.

items.question: What makes Jordan's network recurrent, and why did he build it?
items.answer:
Jordan's network is recurrent because it sends its own output back into part of its input. It copies the output into the state units. So what it produced at one moment helps predict the next moment.

Jordan built it because speech production changes over time. Features such as nasality and lip rounding switch on and off at different moments. So he needed a network that could follow these changes step by step.

items.question: How is a recurrent network different from an nn.Sequential network?
items.answer: A recurrent network is different from an nn.Sequential network because it loops its output back into its input. A Sequential network passes the input through the layers once, from the input to the output, and makes one decision. A recurrent network sends its output back in as part of its next input. So a recurrent network works through a sequence step by step.

items.question: How does GPT use the same idea as Jordan's network?
items.answer: GPT uses the same idea as Jordan's network because it also feeds its own output back into its input. It predicts the next word and adds that word to the prompt. Then it predicts again, using the longer prompt. So GPT produces text one word at a time.

items.question: An LLM is given 15 vectors and predicts the sixteenth. Name three things the vectors can stand for.
items.answer: Three things the vectors can stand for are the words of a sentence, the frames of a spectrogram and the patches of an image. They can also stand for the amino acids of a protein. The same kind of prediction works for all of them. This is because the LLM only works with lists of numbers, whatever those numbers stand for.

items.question: What does the sixteenth vector look like, and does it add up to anything?
items.answer:
The sixteenth vector is a probability distribution over what could come next, and its numbers add up to one.

The sixteenth vector has one number for each possible next item, such as each English word. Each number is how likely that item is to come next.

It adds up to one because it is a probability distribution. The probabilities of all the possible next items always add up to one.

items.question: Why is the next word barks and not bark in "the dog that my parents, who I love very much, ... "?
items.answer: The next word is barks and not bark because barks goes with the singular word dog. This is true no matter how many words come in between. It holds even when the plural word parents comes in between. To predict barks, an LLM has to use a word far back in the sequence. It learns to do this from data, by computing inner products layer after layer.

items.question: Why can an LLM hallucinate?
items.answer: An LLM can hallucinate because it predicts from past data. When it meets something its data does not cover, its prediction can turn into a guess. So it can make things up, and this is called hallucination.

items.question: Describe the Gestalt principle of closure, and how an LLM uses it to learn.
items.answer:
The Gestalt principle of closure is completing a familiar pattern that is not quite finished. For example, people see a triangle where none is drawn, and they see a broken circle as a whole circle.

An LLM (large language model) uses closure to learn by doing the same kind of completion. It predicts the missing next piece of a sequence again and again. When its prediction is wrong, it corrects its weights. So it learns by completing sequences over and over.

items.question: What is a cloze test, and why is an LLM's training like one?
items.answer:
A cloze test is a test where words are removed from a text and people fill them in. So it tests knowledge by asking someone to complete a sequence.

An LLM's training is like a cloze test because the LLM (large language model) is trained by filling in the next word over and over. So for an LLM, knowing something means being able to complete the sequence.

items.question: Why do people see a triangle in the Gestalt figure?
items.answer: People see a triangle in the Gestalt figure because they complete the missing parts of a familiar pattern. No triangle is actually drawn, but people fill in what is missing. This completion is the Gestalt principle of closure.

items.question: In the classroom of experts, what are the classes and what are the students?
items.answer: In the classroom of experts, the classes are the layers and the students are the heads. This is because you visit the classes one after another, just as the layers come one after another. The students in each class each give a separate opinion at the same time, just as the heads in one layer work side by side. You combine those opinions before moving on to the next class. So each class is one layer, and each student in it is one head.

items.question: Which gives an LLM depth and which gives it width, heads or layers?
items.answer: Layers give an LLM depth, and heads give it width. This is because layers are rounds of improvement that come one after another, which adds depth. Heads work side by side inside the same layer, which adds width. So more layers means more rounds, and more heads means more experts in each round.

items.question: An LLM has 5 layers with 4 heads in each layer. How many heads does it have, and which of them work at the same time?
items.answer: The LLM has 20 heads, and the 4 heads inside the same layer work at the same time. This is because each of the 5 layers has 4 heads, and 5 times 4 is 20. The 4 heads inside one layer work side by side. The layers come one after another, so layer 2 works on the vectors that layer 1 improved. So heads in the same layer work at the same time, but heads in different layers do not.

items.question: The LLM predicts bark instead of barks after "the dog that my parents ... ". Which weights change?
items.answer: When the LLM predicts bark instead of barks, the weights of every head in every layer change. This is because backpropagation calculates how much each weight contributed to the wrong prediction. Then each weight is adjusted a little in the direction that reduces the error. So the next prediction is closer to barks.

items.question: Where is the knowledge of an LLM stored?
items.answer: The knowledge of an LLM is stored in its weights. This is because each head is a set of weights, and those weights are what change when the model learns. So the knowledge is spread across all the heads in all the layers. The vowel network's knowledge is stored in its weights in the same way.

items.question: Why is an LLM called a dynamical system?
items.answer: An LLM is called a dynamical system because it works by giving a rule its own output again and again. A dynamical system is a rule that is repeatedly given its own output as input, starting from initial conditions (the starting numbers). In an LLM, the input vectors are the initial conditions. Each layer applies its weights to turn those vectors into better vectors, and the next layer takes those as its input. So the depth of the layers plays the role of time.

items.question: In the harmonic oscillator, which two numbers update, and in what order?
items.answer: In the harmonic oscillator, position x and velocity v update, and they take turns. First, the new x is calculated from the old v. Then, the new v is calculated from the new x. When these two steps are repeated over and over, x traces out a cosine shape.

items.question: After which start is the next-letter distribution flatter, ra_ or skr_? Why?
items.answer: The next-letter distribution is flatter after ra than after skr. This is because ra ends in a vowel, and after a vowel almost any letter can come next. So the probability is spread out over many letters. After skr, only a vowel can come next. So most of the probability goes to a few vowels, and the distribution is sharply peaked.

items.question: Why is Atlantic an English word but tlantic impossible?
items.answer: Atlantic is an English word, but tlantic is impossible. This is because in Atlantic, the t and l are on opposite sides of a syllable break (At-lan-tic), so each syllable follows the rules. In tlantic, tl would have to start a syllable. English does not allow tl at the start of a syllable, so tlantic is impossible.

items.question: Could ngop be an English word? Could flim?
items.answer:
Ngop could not be an English word. This is because the sound ng can end a syllable, as in ring, but it can never start one.

Flim could be an English word. This is because fl is an allowed onset (the consonants before the vowel), as in flat, and im is an allowed ending.

items.question: Why does a GPT trained only to guess the next letter end up knowing English syllable structure?
items.answer: A GPT trained only to guess the next letter ends up knowing English syllable structure because the patterns of English syllables determine which letters can come next. This is because its guesses can only get better by matching those patterns. So as it learns, its probability distributions take on the shape of those patterns. They are flat after a vowel and sharply peaked after a start such as skr.

items.question: Which letter cannot come next after sp_ at the start of a word: l, r, n or a?
items.answer: N cannot come next after sp at the start of a word. This is because spn is not an allowed English onset (the consonants before the vowel). After sp, only l, r or a vowel can come next, as in split, spring and spa.

items.question: Which letter cannot come next after k_ at the start of a word: a, n or t?
items.answer: T cannot come next after k at the start of a word. This is because kt cannot start an English syllable. After k, a vowel or n can come next, as in knee.

items.question: What can come next after b_ or f_ at the start of a word, and what cannot?
items.answer: After b or f at the start of a word, only r, l or a vowel can come next, as in bring, black, frog and flat. N cannot come next. This is because bn and fn cannot start an English syllable.

items.question: What can come next after sh_ at the start of a word?
items.answer: After sh at the start of a word, only a vowel or r can come next, as in ship and shrimp. This is because shr is the only consonant cluster that English allows starting with sh.

items.question: What can come next after skr_?
items.answer: After skr, only a vowel can come next, as in scream and scrap (where the skr sound is spelled scr). This is because skr already fills the whole onset (the consonants before the vowel). So no other consonant can be added before the vowel.

items.question: Why are lfat, hepl and lapm impossible when flat, help and lamp are words?
items.answer: Lfat, hepl and lapm are impossible because the order of a cluster is a mirror image around the vowel. In flat and help, the l sits right next to the vowel. In lamp, the m sits right next to the vowel. Each impossible version puts the wrong consonant next to the vowel. So it breaks the mirror order, and it cannot be an English word.

items.question: Is ship a consonant, vowel, consonant word even though it has four letters?
items.answer: Yes, ship is a consonant, vowel, consonant word even though it has four letters. This is because the pattern is about sounds, not letters, and sh is one sound. So ship is the consonant sh, the vowel i and the consonant p.

items.question: What would happen if the critic LLM were removed?
items.answer: If the critic LLM were removed, the draft would go straight from writing to the final answer without being checked. This is because the critic is the LLM that checks the draft. So more made-up statements would reach the user. The critic loop is what greatly reduced hallucination, so without it that reduction would be lost.

items.question: What is the difference between Software 2.0 and Software 3.0?
items.answer:
The difference between Software 2.0 and Software 3.0 is how the program gets built.

In Software 2.0, a neural network is trained on input and output data, so the program is the network's weights.

In Software 3.0, an agentic system builds and runs the program from plain English instructions. Building a program this way is called vibe coding.

sets.title: Lecture 19 · new slides · 27 predicted questions
sets.about: Written from Lecture 19 pages 9 to 19 in the way he asks questions. These are predictions, not confirmed exam questions.

items.question: How does an LLM learn from the sentence "The chef cracks the ?"
items.answer:
An LLM learns from this sentence by guessing the hidden last word and then changing its weights a little.

This is because each word before the gap gives a clue about the hidden word. So the model bets the most on "egg," less on "nut" and the least on "code." When the true word is revealed, the weights are nudged. So the right word gets a bigger bet next time.

items.question: Why does the model give "egg," "nut" and "code" different bets instead of one answer?
items.answer: The model gives three different bets because it does not know the hidden word. All three words could follow "The chef cracks the." The words before the gap make "egg" the most likely. So "egg" gets the largest bet, "nut" gets a smaller bet and "code" gets the smallest bet.

items.question: What does learning change in an LLM, and in which direction?
items.answer: Learning changes the weights. Each weight is nudged, which means it changes a little. The weights change in the direction that gives the right word a bigger bet the next time.

items.question: Why is text easier for an LLM to read than speech or an image?
items.answer:
Text is easier because it is already a row of pieces. Each piece, such as "Now," "crack," "the" or "egg," can become one vector.

Speech is air pressure changing in time, and an image is a grid of light. Neither one contains words or separate pieces. So both have to be converted into rows of vectors first.

items.question: How is speech turned into a row of vectors?
items.answer: Speech is turned into a row of vectors by slicing it in time. First, the sound is cut into short slices called frames, each about 20 milliseconds long. Then the slices go through a speech encoder, which is a neural network trained on a large amount of audio. One vector comes out for each slice, and the vectors stay in time order.

items.question: Why does one second of speech become 50 vectors?
items.answer: One second of speech becomes 50 vectors because each slice gives one vector. Each slice is about 20 milliseconds long, and 50 slices of that length fill one second. So one second gives 50 vectors.

items.question: How is an image turned into a row of vectors?
items.answer: An image is turned into a row of vectors by cutting it into patches. First, a grid cuts the image into small squares called patches. Then the patches are laid out in a row in reading order, so the image becomes a sequence. Last, a vision encoder gives one vector for each patch.

items.question: The egg example gives 16 vectors. Why does one image give hundreds of vectors in real systems?
items.answer: One image gives hundreds of vectors in real systems because real systems use much smaller patches. Their patches are only 14 to 16 pixels. Smaller patches mean more patches for the same image. Each patch gives one vector, so there are hundreds of vectors.

items.question: What is the similarity between converting speech and converting an image, and what is the difference?
items.answer:
The similarity is that both are cut into small pieces, the pieces are kept in order, and an encoder gives one vector for each piece.

The difference is what is cut. Speech is cut in time into frames of about 20 milliseconds. An image is cut in space into square patches, which are then placed in reading order.

items.question: What is a cross-modal dependency? Give an example.
items.answer:
A cross-modal dependency is a link between two different kinds of signal, in which a piece from one sense helps predict a piece from another sense.

For example, in "Now crack the ?", an image patch that contains an egg helps the model guess the hidden word. The sound of cracking helps too.

items.question: When image patches and speech frames are added to the row, what stays the same and what changes?
items.answer:
The game stays the same. The model still guesses the hidden piece from the pieces it can read, and the words before the gap still give clues.

What changes is where some of the clues come from. Some clues now come from image patches and speech frames.

items.question: In the spectrogram of "three cute puppies," what do left to right, height and darkness mean?
items.answer: Left to right is time, so "three" comes first and "puppies" comes last. Height is frequency, so higher up means a higher frequency. Darkness is energy, so a darker area means more energy. Each thin column is one frame.

items.question: Why are the image, the spectrogram and the words called three views of one event?
items.answer: They are called three views of one event because all three describe the same thing, which is three cute puppies. The image gives it as patches, the speech gives it as frames, and the text gives it as words. In training, all three go into one row.

items.question: How do the model's bets on the next word change when the image and the sound are added to "three cute"?
items.answer:
With the words alone, the bets are spread out over "kittens," "puppies" and "babies." This is because many endings fit after "three cute."

With the image and the sound, the bet piles up on "puppies." This is because the image contains puppies, and the sound contains the spoken word "puppies."

items.question: The model bet 0.85 on "puppies," and the true word is "puppies." Is the nudge to the weights large or small? Why?
items.answer: The nudge to the weights is small. This is because the model is graded on how much it bet on the true word. It bet 0.85, which is a lot, so the error is small. A small error moves the weights only a little.

items.question: What would happen to the nudge if the model had bet only a little on "puppies"?
items.answer: The nudge would be larger. This is because a small bet on the true word is a large error. A larger error moves the weights more, so that the true word gets a bigger bet next time.

items.question: Name the three clues that help the model predict a hidden sound frame, and say what each one gives.
items.answer:
The first clue is the frames already heard. The voice and the formants change smoothly, so the last few frames say a lot about the next one.

The second clue is the words. They say which sound should come next, which here is the vowel in "pup."

The third clue is the image. It contains puppies, so it backs up the words, but it is a weaker clue here.

items.question: What is the error when the model guesses a sound frame?
items.answer: The error is how far the guess is from the true frame. A frame is a column of numbers, and each number is how much energy there is in one frequency band. The error is how far apart each guessed number is from the matching true number. That error nudges the weights.

items.question: In training example 3, why is the colour the biggest error?
items.answer: The colour is the biggest error because no clue gave the colour of the third puppy. The model guessed a puppy ear in the average colour of the first two puppies. The true puppy is dark. Nothing in the words, the sound or the patches already drawn said the third puppy would be dark.

items.question: What do the words "three" and "puppies" tell the model about the hidden image patch?
items.answer: "Three" tells the model that a third puppy must appear, because only two puppies have been drawn so far. "Puppies" tells the model to expect dog ears. So the model guesses a puppy ear for the hidden patch.

items.question: Are all systems trained to predict image patches?
items.answer: No. Only systems that also produce images are trained to predict image patches. Systems that only read images usually skip this step. This is because predicting a patch is like teaching the model to draw what it was told.

items.question: What is the difference between a clue from the same sense as the hidden piece and a clue from another sense?
items.answer:
A clue from the same sense mostly says how the signal continues. Grammar does this for a hidden word, smooth formants do it for a hidden frame, and fur and background do it for a hidden patch.

Clues from the other senses mostly say what the thing is. Here they say puppies, three of them.

items.question: For a hidden sound frame, which clue comes from the same sense, and what does it tell the model?
items.answer: The clue from the same sense is that the voice and the formants carry on from the frames already heard. It tells the model how the sound continues. The words and the image are the other senses, and they say which word is being said.

items.question: Why does training on words, sound and images together help?
items.answer: Training on all three senses together helps because each sense fills gaps that the others leave. A clue from the same sense says how the signal continues. Clues from the other senses say what the thing is. So with all three senses, the model has both kinds of clue for every hidden piece.

items.question: How does the model talk back?
items.answer: The model talks back by predicting codes for sound. First, sound is compressed into discrete codes, and each code works like a new word in the vocabulary. Then the model predicts the next code exactly as it predicts the next word. Last, a decoder turns the codes back into a sound wave.

items.question: What three things are new when an LLM is trained on words, sounds and images?
items.answer: The first new thing is a shared currency, in which everything becomes vectors in one row. The second is data where the senses appear together. The third is a schedule that protects what was already learned.

items.question: What stays the same when the signal holds words, sounds and images?
items.answer: The learning rule stays the same. The model still finds the dependencies in the signal by guessing a hidden piece and nudging its weights. The signal has only become wider.
